column7: Shin-ei's own historical page identifies the Honey Co. Ltd. FY-6 Baby Crying as released in 1967 and as the first incarnation of the Super Fuzz line.
column10: Treat Honey as the original branded product state; later Shin-ei and Univox forms remain separate retail objects.

column7: Shin-ei identifies the FY-6 Super Fuzz as the 1968 follow-up to the 1967 Honey Baby Crying Fuzz, with the Shin-ei label distinguishing the branded production state.
column10: Use the 1968 label transition as a firm branding clue, not as proof that every FY-6 part changed simultaneously.

column7: The early Univox Super-Fuzz was imported by Unicord and is documented in grey stamped-metal form; the U-1093 designation is associated with the early grey state.
column10: Do not collapse U-1093 and U-1095 into one specimen state; enclosure and U.S. market evidence support a distinction.

column7: The later Univox Super-Fuzz moved into a die-cast enclosure with the large Super-Fuzz footpad; production continued through the 1970s.
column10: Exact transition date should remain approximate until specimen/date-stamp evidence is reconciled.

column7: The Companion FY-2 is a separate Shin-ei fuzz model from the FY-6 Super Fuzz family, documented from the late 1960s into the early 1970s.
column10: Do not identify FY-2 as an FY-6 variant; the two are separate model families sharing the broader Shin-ei/Honey history.

column7: Recent specialist research documents an early germanium FY-2 state distinct from later silicon examples; the early version is rarer and warrants specimen-level treatment.
column10: Keep the germanium/silicon distinction research-level until a broader dated specimen census is assembled.

column7: Whotabs documents the Shaftesbury Duo Fuzz as a Shin-ei-made Japanese pedal badged for Rose-Morris for the UK market and essentially a rebranded FY-6 Super Fuzz.
column10: Preserve Rose-Morris/Shaftesbury as the UK retail/import layer and Shin-ei as the documented manufacturer.

column7: Tone Machines Blog documents the Royal Fuzz Box TF-1 / RF-1 as a 1969 Japanese FY-6-related product and distinguishes it from straightforward later rebranding.
column10: Treat Royal as a distinct branded/production state; exact manufacturer attribution remains unresolved.

column7: The Teisco TF-1 is documented as a Japanese FY-6 Super Fuzz family product and should not be confused with Teisco's separately branded Fuzz Machine lineage.
column10: Use model name, control arrangement and enclosure as identification clues.

column7: Effects Database places the Teisco Wau Wau Fuzz in a Japanese OEM wah-fuzz family alongside the Ibanez Wau Wau Fuzz, Guyatone FS-5 and Elk Wau Fuzz.
column10: Likely Shin-ei/related OEM attribution remains probabilistic; keep the family link separate from definitive manufacturer claims.

column7: Guyatone catalogs and specialist research place the FS-3 between the FS-2 and FS-6, with surviving examples using a Honey-marked board associated with the Super Fuzz family.
column10: Chronology is strong; the identity of the party that built the pedal remains unresolved.

column7: Specialist research notes that the 1972 Guyatone catalog places the FS-5 Wah-Fuzz beside the FS-4 and identifies those wah products as Maxon-made, while the broader OEM family includes multiple rebadged versions.
column10: Preserve the Maxon attribution as a research-backed manufacturing lead rather than a fully resolved chain of custody.

column7: Effects Database documents the Ace Tone FM-1 as an early Japanese Fuzz Master with volume and fuzz-adjust controls; period research distinguishes it from the later FM-2.
column10: Keep FM-1 and FM-2 as separate models even though period naming can appear inconsistent.

column7: Tone Machines Blog found a May 1968 newspaper reference to the Fuzz Master name and a 1971 ad explicitly showing the FM-2, making 1968 a strong early evidence point rather than the older 1969 estimate.
column10: Preserve 1968 as an early documentation point; exact launch date and production endpoint remain open.

column7: Modern historical review sources place the Ace Tone FM-3 around 1971 and identify it as an early Japanese Big Muff-related design distinct from the FM-2 Super Fuzz-type model.
column10: Do not merge FM-3 with FM-2; the family relationship is through the Ace Tone line, not a shared circuit identity.

column7: Vintage Guitar documents the U-250 Uni-Fuzz as a separate Univox fuzz model alongside the U-1093/U-1095 Super-Fuzz, with Univox's Japanese Shin-ei/OEM relationships continuing through the 1970s.
column10: Keep U-250 separate from the FY-6 Super-Fuzz family until its manufacturing lineage is independently reconciled.
